proof:
# Joint complements select original-cap groups and retain their overlap costs

Let S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) be nonempty, let q=dim_H S, and use
mu=H_q restricted to S. Let P be the finite set of q-dimensional
integer fibers K_z, with w_z=H_q(K_z)>0 and M=sum_z w_z. Put m=2^n.
For n=0 interpret m=1. Lower-dimensional fibers carry zero mu mass;
when q=0 all nonempty fibers are singleton fibers and are retained.

Fix actual CLOSED ambient caps H_1,...,H_N. For every nonempty index
set I subset {1,...,N}, write

  U_I=union_(i in I) H_i,
  E_I(z)=K_z intersect intersection_(i in I) (H_i)_z^c,
  e_I(z)=H_q(E_I(z)),
  B_I=mu(U_I).

Thus every remainder is an actual COMMON intersection of strict cap
complements. We do not replace it by the separate individual masses.

## 1. Joint positive and absolute-threshold supports are integer convex

For t>0 each of the finite base sets

  Q_I(t)={z in P:e_I(z)>=t},
  Q_I^+={z in P:e_I(z)>0}

equals the integer points of its convex hull. For q>=1 the proof is
the dimension-tracked Brunn--Minkowski argument from
`candidate af89470c3209e9d8`, now retaining
EVERY inequality in I simultaneously. Take compact convex inner
approximants of positive q-volume in each E_I(z_l). Their Minkowski
combination remains strictly outside every cap of I, by affinity,
and lies in the integer target fiber. Its dimension is at least q
and at most the maximal intrinsic dimension q. Therefore all source
direction spaces coincide with one q-dimensional space, and

  e_I(sum_l alpha_l z_l)^(1/q)
     >=sum_l alpha_l e_I(z_l)^(1/q)                     (1)

at every integer target in question. Compact inner approximation
preserves all finitely many strict inequalities and recovers their
full remainder measure. This proves both assertions. For q=0, a
convex combination of strictly negative singleton points preserves
every strict inequality; the integer target fiber is again a
singleton. That is the direct counting-measure proof.

In particular the assertions permit vertical caps, caps constant on
an intrinsic affine fiber, and fibers with different original affine
orientations. A whole fiber on a closed cap boundary is captured.

## 2. Exact original-cap group compression for ANY finite cover

Suppose the original caps cover S, or even only cover it up to a
mu-null set. Then there exist groups I_1,...,I_k such that

  k<=m,    1<=|I_j|<=q+1,                              (2)

and EVERY positive intrinsic fiber K_z is covered ENTIRELY by at
least one of the selected unions U_(I_j).

Proof. A finite closed cap union covering K_z up to q-volume zero
covers the whole K_z: a point outside that union has a relative
neighborhood outside it, and every such neighborhood of a point of
the convex q-body has positive q-volume. For q=0 this is immediate.

Work in the affine hull of K_z. The open convex sets

  relint(K_z) intersect intersection conditions x notin H_i

are most conveniently taken one at a time as
A_i=relint(K_z) intersect H_i^c. Their common intersection is empty.
Finite-dimensional Helly supplies a subfamily I of at most q+1
members with empty intersection. Thus U_I contains relint(K_z),
and its closedness implies K_z subset U_I. The same assertion is
immediate for q=0, where one cap captures the point.

Let G be the finite family of ALL nonempty I with |I|<=q+1 (and
I subset {1,...,N}). The preceding paragraph says intersection_(I in G)
Q_I^+ is empty. Section 1 and Doignon give at most m of the convex
hulls conv(Q_I^+) whose intersection has no integer point. Their
original groups are I_1,...,I_k. At any z in P, one selected group
has e_(I_j)(z)=0. Its finite closed union then covers the WHOLE
fiber by the first paragraph. This proves (2). For n=0 select the
one group supplied directly at the unique positive fiber. QED.

This is a refinement in DATA RETENTION, not a new value of the
mixed Helly number. The earlier
`candidate d2b290ebd8e35052` constructs up to 2^n
groups of d+1 caps for strict depth failures, with whole-space
coverage and circuit contacts. Here every cap is an unchanged
member of an ARBITRARY given finite cover; group size is the
intrinsic q+1; and coverage means the actual K_z, with its supporting
boundary geometry retained. No positive-normal circuit or contact
point is asserted for these groups.

### 2.1 Exact compression of the joint-remainder max-min value

For ANY nonempty finite group family G, not necessarily a cover, set

  V(G)=max_(z in P) min_(I in G) e_I(z).

This attained finite maximum has the exact Helly reduction

  V(G)=min_(J subset G, 1<=|J|<=m)
             max_(z in P) min_(I in J) e_I(z).          (2a)

The easy direction follows because removing groups increases the
inner minimum. For the reverse, put t=V(G). The strict superlevel
sets {z:e_I(z)>t} are lattice-convex by the proof of Section 1, and
their common intersection is empty by the definition of t. Doignon
selects at most m such sets with empty common integer intersection.
For the selected groups every fiber has some e_I(z)<=t, giving the
reverse inequality and an actual attaining subfamily in (2a).
There is no limit of selected fibers or unachieved threshold here.
The same proof allows e_I(z) to be divided by a prescribed positive
constant depending on I. This is an exact scalar selection identity
for joint volumes, not a point-selection theorem inside a fiber.

## 3. Quantitative common JOINT remainders from actual union budgets

Let G now be ANY finite family of nonempty index sets, without a
cover assumption. Let L_m(G) be the sum of its m largest union
masses B_I, or the sum of all of them if |G|<m. Define

  F(t)=sum_(z in P)(w_z-t)_+,
  W=max_z w_z.

If L_m(G)<M and L_m(G)>0, let t_* be the unique solution in (0,W)
to F(t_*)=L_m(G). If L_m(G)=0 set t_*=W. Then ONE actual fiber
satisfies

  e_I(z_*)>=t_* for EVERY I in G.                       (3)

Indeed, if the threshold sets Q_I(t_*) have empty intersection,
Doignon selects at most m of them with empty integer intersection.
At every z some selected group satisfies
mu_z(U_I)>w_z-t_*. Summing the selected union masses gives a strict
total greater than F(t_*): at least one positive-part term exists
when F(t_*)>0. But their sum is at most L_m(G), a contradiction.
For L_m(G)=0 every union has zero mass on every positive fiber, and
any maximum-volume fiber works directly.

The simpler sufficient input B_I<=B_r for every |I|<=r yields
F(t_*)=mB_r whenever mB_r<M. Since B_I are ACTUAL union masses,
overlapping caps may give much smaller B_r than the crude r times
an individual cap budget. Formula (3) guarantees every selected
joint remainder, not a common remainder of all caps unless the
index sets actually include that full intersection.

In particular, for a cover and r=q+1 the family of all such groups
cannot satisfy mB_r<M. Thus every finite cover has SOME group of
at most q+1 ORIGINAL caps whose union has mass at least M/m. This
also follows directly by summing the selected unions in Section 2.

## 4. Exact overlap-sensitive budget consequences

For the selected groups in Section 2, put

  k_j=|I_j|,    K=sum_j k_j<=m(q+1),
  D_j=sum_(i in I_j) mu(H_i)-mu(U_(I_j))
     =int (sum_(i in I_j)1_(H_i)-1_(U_(I_j))) dmu>=0.

Every fiber is wholly covered by some selected union, hence

  M+sum_j D_j <= sum_j sum_(i in I_j) mu(H_i).           (4)

If individual cap masses are at most B, this gives

  B >= (M+sum_j D_j)/K
      >= (M+sum_j D_j)/[m(q+1)].                        (5)

Reused caps are counted with their occurrences. All overlaps are
actual closed intersections in the original measure. For example,
D_j can be evaluated by exact finite inclusion-exclusion; no
independence or disjointness approximation is used.

A useful explicit weaker form needs only pair intersections. For
any spanning tree T on a group I, pointwise

  1_(U_I)<=sum_(i in I)1_(H_i)
                 -sum_({i,l} in T)1_(H_i intersect H_l). (6)

To prove it, at a point covered by h>=1 group caps, the tree induced
on those h active vertices is a forest with at most h-1 edges. At
an uncovered point all terms vanish. Thus

  mu(U_I)<=sum_(i in I)mu(H_i)
                   -max_T sum_({i,l} in T)mu(H_i intersect H_l).

If every pair of distinct original caps overlaps in mass at least
delta, where 0<=delta<=B, then for |I|=k<=q+1,

  mu(U_I)<=kB-(k-1)delta
          <=(q+1)B-q delta.

The large-union conclusion in Section 3 consequently implies

  B >= M/[m(q+1)] + q delta/(q+1).                     (7)

For example, on the single interval [-1,1] with caps x>=-epsilon
and x<=epsilon, 0<=epsilon<=1, the overlap has mass delta=2epsilon
and both cap masses equal 1+epsilon. Bound (7) gives exactly
B>=1+epsilon, whereas the individual absolute-remainder bound with
no overlap input gives only B>=1. This calibrates the correction;
it does not turn the simple overlap algebra into a new universal
gamma bound.

This is a genuine overlap correction to the cardinality estimate,
but it is NOT claimed to imply gamma_q M/m for arbitrary cap data.
The algebraic multiplicity identity itself is familiar and was also
used for continuous circuits in
`candidate ebf5465656e86ce1`.
The new input here is selecting groups of UNCHANGED original caps
for any cover, with whole actual-fiber ownership and intrinsic q.
The earlier zero-charge example also warns that compatibility alone
cannot force D_j to have a uniform positive lower bound.

## 5. Sharpness of grouping, and a limit of pairwise extrapolation

Both the group count m and the maximum group size q+1 can be
simultaneously necessary. Take C=[0,1]^n x K, with K a q-simplex
and d=q>=1. At each binary base v use its q+1 barycentric centroid
caps {alpha_i>=1/(q+1)}, with a sufficiently large integer-coordinate
tilt isolating that base. Explicitly, with
A_v(z)=sum_l(2v_l-1)(z_l-v_l), use

  alpha_i(x)+2 A_v(z)>=1/(q+1).

At v these are the indicated simplex caps; at another binary base
the left side is at most 1-2<0. They cover S. Covering a given
fiber requires all its q+1 own caps, since each is uniquely needed
near its corresponding simplex vertex. Therefore any grouping with
at most q+1 caps per group and whole-fiber coverage needs exactly
m groups. Each such group is that fiber's own complete cap family.
The q=0 counting example is the binary cube with individually
isolating vertical caps.

It is also false that positive pairwise joint remainders force a
positive all-cap remainder. Already for a single planar triangle
take its three centroid caps H_i={alpha_i>=1/3}. Their complements
are STRICT. The individual remainders have fraction 5/9, each
two-cap common remainder has fraction 2/9, and the three-cap common
remainder is empty because sum alpha_i=1. The pairwise common
remainders are actual convex portions of the same triangle, not
artificially prescribed masses. Thus using groups of size q+1 is
essential for the exact cover-selection step; pairwise positive
remainders alone cannot certify a surviving point when q=2.

No unproved gamma allocation, common point inferred from individual
remainders, or equivalent reformulation of OC is used here.
